reading.title: Along the Cedar Creek Trail
reading.purpose: Walk with a student volunteer team restoring a creek that once fed an old mill town.
paras: Saturday fog still clung to the willows as eighth grader Luis stepped off the bus with a bundle of native sedge plugs. Fifty years ago, factories along Cedar Creek had tried to exploit the valley—using its water and timber selfishly for quick profit without thinking about tomorrow. Heavy logging and untreated waste had begun to degrade the stream banks, wearing down water quality until local salamanders nearly vanished.

"Fresh water and healthy soil are finite," explained Ms. Okafor, the watershed director, pointing to a gauge in the gravel. "They have real limits. If a town acts as though nature is endless, it can exhaust its clean aquifers before anyone notices." She reminded the volunteers that several mussel species once common in the county were now completely extinct, gone forever because their gravel beds had silted over.

Luis knelt beside his partner Hannah to plant deep-rooted grasses along the muddy bend. Every cluster would help mitigate storm runoff, making muddy floods less severe by trapping dirt before it reached the water. Up on the visitor shed, solar panels caught the pale morning sun, supplying renewable power that nature replenishes every day without pouring another dark emission of smoke or soot into the valley air.

By noon, forty students had stabilized a hundred yards of shoreline. Luis wiped mud from his sleeves and looked back down the curving creek. Real conservation, he realized, was not about locking nature behind a fence; it was active stewardship—caring responsibly for a shared place so the next generation inherits a living river instead of a dry ditch.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "mitigate" most nearly means
choices: to use up every drop of water inside an underground aquifer
to make a harmful problem less severe or less damaging
to release dark smoke and soot from a valley factory stack
to measure the depth of a stream using a metal gravel gauge
qs.why: Paragraph 3 defines mitigate directly as "making muddy floods less severe by trapping dirt before it reached the water."

qs.q: Which sentence shows why several local mussel species disappeared permanently?
choices: If a town acts as though nature is endless, it can exhaust its clean aquifers before anyone notices.
She reminded the volunteers that several mussel species once common in the county were now completely extinct, gone forever because their gravel beds had silted over.
By noon, forty students had stabilized a hundred yards of shoreline.
qs.why: This sentence names the exact cause of the mussels' extinction: their gravel beds had silted over.

ev.text: She reminded the volunteers that several mussel species once common in the county were now completely extinct, gone forever because their gravel beds had silted over.

qs.q: What does Luis mean when he thinks conservation is "not about locking nature behind a fence"?
choices: Protecting land takes hands-on care and restoration, not just keeping people away.
Metal fences around Cedar Creek are too expensive for a watershed director to buy.
Factories should be allowed to return to the valley as long as they plant grasses.
Solar panels work better when students build visitor sheds beside muddy trails.
qs.why: Luis contrasts locking nature behind a fence with "active stewardship—caring responsibly for a shared place," like planting sedge to stabilize the bank.

qs.q: What is the main theme of this story?
choices: Once a creek has been harmed by old logging, volunteers cannot repair its banks.
Responsible stewardship and clean energy can help communities heal damaged natural resources.
Salamanders are much easier to protect than freshwater mussels in shallow streams.
Eighth graders learn more about science from bus rides than from watershed directors.
qs.why: The story contrasts past exploitation with students actively mitigating erosion and practicing stewardship along Cedar Creek.

clues.text: using its water and timber selfishly for quick profit
caring responsibly for a shared place
